slides.title: South Africa remains an import-led fuel market, making customer capture Vopak’s priority
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02 and market-sizing analysis. Demand is estimated; production and capture are planning assumptions. Product reconciliation remains open;

slides.title: Fuel demand has eased to 21.0bn litres and stays broadly flat through 2030 in the base case
side: Eskom: recovery lowers power fuel use.
Road-to-rail and efficiency reduce road fuel use.
Matola: an alternative gateway competes for inland flows.
2030 base: 20.9bn L demand; 16.6bn L gross imports.
slides.takeaway: Demand determines consumption, domestic production determines import need, and competing gateways determine Durban’s share.
slides.source: Department sales 2013–2023; analytical workbook v02. E = estimated 2024–2025. 2030 is the base scenario, not an observed outcome.

slides.title: Petrol has declined since 2013, while diesel has sustained the market
side: Petrol: 9.04bn L in 2023 to 8.86bn L in 2025E.
Assumed efficiency and fleet changes outweigh activity growth.
slides.takeaway: Petrol remains below its earlier level; diesel demand responds more directly to freight, industry and power.
slides.source: Department annual sales, 2013–2023. Estimated 2024–2025: analytical workbook v02. The Department series is used consistently.

slides.title: Road use dominates the baseline, with meaningful diesel demand outside transport
side: Other diesel: 1.91bn L remains unallocated to a specific end use.
slides.takeaway: Sector-attributed vehicle fuel stays in its sector; the road split is an explicit allocation assumption.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Segments. 2021 energy-balance road volume; 75% of road diesel allocated to freight. Historical sector intensities at current activity.

slides.title: The 5.8bn-litre production assumption leaves a gross import requirement of about 16.7bn litres
slides.takeaway: 5.8bn litres sets the planning case. Aggregate closure does not validate domestic output or its petrol/diesel split.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, national demand and trade balance. Domestic production is a planning assumption; the alternative plant-based estimate is retained in the appendix.

slides.title: Agricultural demand rebounds in 2025 while mining and manufacturing remain broadly flat
side: Manufacturing covers the energy-balance industry residual, not a complete industrial census.
slides.takeaway: Sector activity produces different demand paths; applying one GDP growth rate would hide these differences.
slides.source: Stats SA mining/manufacturing indices and agriculture real GVA; mean 2018–2021 fuel intensity. Sector diesel values after 2021 are estimates.

slides.title: Eskom’s fuel use fell by 40% in FY2025 as electricity supply improved
side: Eskom diesel and kerosene fell from 1.130bn L in FY2024 to 0.679bn L in FY2025.
Better supply can also reduce backup diesel at mines, factories and farms.
Private backup use is estimated separately; it is not measured by this Eskom series.
slides.takeaway: Power recovery reduces a source of diesel demand created by electricity shortages; the 2030 assumptions are in the appendix.
slides.source: Eskom Integrated Report 2025, p141. Fiscal years end in March. Reported series includes diesel and kerosene; private backup consumption is outside this series.

slides.title: Rail volumes are recovering, creating scope to reduce road diesel use
side: Rail: 160.7m tonnes in 2024 to 168.3m in 2025. Road: 979.8m to 976.5m tonnes.
A shift of mining, agricultural and manufactured goods to rail can reduce truck fuel use.
Rail growth alone does not prove road displacement; distance, cargo and traction mix matter.
slides.takeaway: Road remains the dominant freight mode; sustained rail recovery could change the diesel required to move goods.
slides.source: Stats SA P7162 December 2025 p7; all reported freight. Analytical workbook v02, Evidence.

slides.title: Changes in refinery output alter the volume that imports must supply
rows: Refined-products output: 29.1m barrels in FY2024; 27.6m in FY2025; 30.6m in FY2026
Operating recovery can increase domestic supply; petrol and diesel yields determine import displacement.
Sasol-reported output: 17.8m barrels in FY2024; 14.7m in FY2025; 25.8m in FY2026
FY2026 includes above-share production, so the latest reported change cannot be treated as a like-for-like change in whole-plant output.
Reported refined products: 166,204 billion Btu in 2024; 164,365 billion Btu in 2025
Output and product mix affect supply; energy units require conversion before comparison with customs litres.
No refining contribution included in the 2025 production assessment
Restored refining would displace imports only when plants produce saleable products. Terminal handling is not refinery output.
slides.takeaway: Domestic production can recover or fall independently of demand; actual output and product yields determine the import requirement.
slides.source: Sasol production metrics FY2025 and FY2026; Glencore annual reports 2024 and 2025; 2025 plant assessment. Fiscal and calendar periods and reporting scopes differ. Restart sensitivities are in the appendix.

slides.title: Matola provides an existing alternative gateway for inland fuel supply
headers: Implication for South African fuel routes
rows: Broader storage base; product allocation and overlap need confirmation
Regional supply; no additional SA flow assigned in the base case
Light oil, gas and LPG; production began December 2025
No direct finished petrol/diesel output credited
Current cross-border flow is far smaller than gross storage suggests
slides.takeaway: Matola’s infrastructure creates an alternative supply route; recorded cross-border flows remain much smaller than storage capacity.
slides.source: Galp Matola commissioning release, 3 December 2020; Petromoc logistics disclosures; Sasol Mozambique operations; SARS customs, 2022 and 2025. Storage is not annual throughput.

slides.title: The base case leaves imports near 16.6bn litres in 2030, with refinery recovery driving the downside
side: Cases are sensitivities, not assigned probabilities.
slides.takeaway: The base case balances activity growth against efficiency, rail and power reductions; supply assumptions drive the widest spread.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Scenarios. Demand-implied gross imports = demand − domestic supply + 2025 exports. Zero stock change; 5.8bn L assumed opening supply.

slides.title: Vopak’s capture depends on the accessible share of Durban imports
rows: Gateway proxy before customer and route allocation
20% of Durban gateway volume; no contracted share inferred
50% of captured Durban flow; counted within the same fuel volume
slides.takeaway: The illustrative unique flow is 2.63bn litres. Adding Lesedi would double-count fuel handled at both sites.
slides.source: Market-sizing analysis, October 2026. Capture is total conditional flow, not incremental sales; domestic and other-terminal Lesedi receipts are outside this screen.

slides.title: The illustrative capture case fits the tank-turn screen, making usable capacity the next test
rows: 124,000m³ working capacity, partly estimated; two turns/month
Receipt, product segregation, dispatch, pipeline access and peak demand
slides.takeaway: Working-tank arithmetic screens feasibility. Engineering limits and current customer flows determine actual headroom.
slides.source: Terminal working-capacity assessment, October 2026. Durban working subset is not the full terminal; access, peaks and current throughput remain open.

slides.title: The market supports an import platform; customer capture and capacity constraints govern investment
rows: Prioritise identifiable customer segments and destinations
About 16.6bn litres in 2030 under the 5.8bn supply case
Plan for ongoing imports; retain refinery sensitivities
Gateways compete for the same fuel
Mozambique base diversion of 0.20bn L is a route assumption
Validate delivered cost, service and customer access
Illustrative 2.63bn L unique flow fits the tank-turn screen
Secure additional volumes, prove the bottleneck, then compare improvement and expansion returns
slides.takeaway: Next decisions: review the product balance, obtain route quotes and customer commitments, and establish usable capacity at both sites.
slides.source: 2025 analytical workbook v02: demand assumptions and 5.8bn L domestic production case. Estimates are not reported actuals.

slides.title: Appendix
Further power recovery halves fuel demand to 0.54bn litres in the 2030 base case
side: 2025 estimate: 1.08bn L, including 0.20bn L assumed private backup.
Base: 50% retained in 2030; a 0.54bn L reduction.
Lower-use case: 35% retained. Unchanged-use case: 100% retained.
slides.takeaway: Improved electricity supply lowers peaking and backup fuel use, even where transport and industrial activity continue to grow.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02: calculated power baseline and 2030 retention assumptions. Estimated utility/private scope includes FY proxies and IPP conversion. Scenario endpoints, not forecasts of annual dispatch.

slides.title: A 7.5% shift of road-freight activity to rail saves 0.33bn litres in the base case
slides.takeaway: These shifts apply to road-freight activity, not the entire diesel market; sector demand and power remain separate.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Driver bridge and scenario assumptions. Shift interpreted as freight tonne-km share. Distances and eligibility remain assumed; cases also vary growth and efficiency.

slides.title: Refinery restart assumptions drive the lower-import sensitivity
rows: 15% increase in the national planning volume
Assumed 2029 start; 65% utilisation after a two-year ramp
Assumed 2029 start; 50% utilisation after a two-year ramp
slides.takeaway: Restart dates and ramp-up settings are scenario assumptions. Import-terminal operations can compete before refining resumes.
slides.source: Refinery production and restart scenario assumptions. Capacity inputs: SAPREF 180kb/d, PetroSA 45kb/d; 70% petrol/diesel yield in restart sensitivities. Dates are not project commitments.

slides.title: Illustrative route costs put Matola at a R0.19-per-litre logistics premium
rows: 600km one way; round trip; R25/truck-km; 40,000L payload
550km one way; terminal and border costs; one-day delay
Required landed-product discount under these illustrative costs
About 15 additional loaded trucks/day over 330 days
slides.takeaway: Mozambique diversion changes the gateway serving demand. It does not reduce South Africa’s national import requirement.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Mozambique. Distances, tariffs, border charges, financing and allocation are illustrative sensitivities, not carrier quotes or confirmed access.

slides.title: The national supply assumption closes the total balance but leaves the product mix unresolved
slides.takeaway: The 5.8bn L planning case uses the original estimated production mix. Offsetting product differences remain visible; no product allocation is claimed as verified.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Supply assumption and Balance. Original plant estimate: Secunda 3.95, Natref 2.37, Astron 3.91bn L; 10.23bn total. These do not govern the planning case.

slides.title: Efficiency offsets activity growth in the petrol baseline
rows: A combined efficiency / fleet-mix assumption reduces fuel per unit of activity
Compounding activity and intensity yields a modest decline
Applied after activity growth; rail displacement is then applied to freight only
slides.takeaway: The assumptions are explicit and editable; EV uptake is not counted again as a separate reduction.
slides.source: Department 2023 sales; analytical workbook v02, Assumptions and Demand history. Activity and efficiency settings are illustrative planning assumptions.

slides.title: Our 2025 baseline is 21.0bn litres, with road use accounting for most demand
slides.takeaway: Petrol: 8.86bn L. Diesel: 12.13bn L. Total demand falls from 21.94bn L in 2023 to an estimated 20.99bn L in 2025.
slides.source: Department sales through 2023; energy balances and Stats SA activity; Eskom/IPP evidence. All 2025 segment allocations are estimates; other diesel retains an explicit residual.

slides.title: Source definitions and explicit assumptions underpin the demand and import outlook
rows: Department sales, energy balances and Stats SA activity. Demand after 2023 is estimated; segment boundaries retain an unallocated residual.
Eskom fuel and Stats SA freight observations. Private backup, future rail shift and efficiency remain explicit planning assumptions.
Sasol and Glencore plant disclosures; SARS trade. The 5.8bn-litre national production case is an assumption; product reconciliation remains open.
Operator infrastructure disclosures and SARS customs. Logistics costs are illustrative, rather than carrier quotations.
Illustrative gateway capture and working-tank turnover. Customer commitments and engineering constraints determine achievable volumes.
slides.takeaway: Observed data, estimates and scenario assumptions are labelled separately throughout the analysis.
slides.source: Sources: Department energy statistics; Stats SA; Eskom; Sasol; Glencore; SARS; Galp; Petromoc. Supporting calculations: analytical workbook v02 and market-sizing workbook.
